extracted.intended_audience: naturalists and general readers interested in travel and natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Composing descriptive travel / natural-history narratives that combine close observational detail (flora, fauna, geology, peoples) with comparative reasoning and broader generalizations about regions and history. Emphasizes framing, specimen-based credibility, and vivid local color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use distribution of species as evidence of past land connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Their presence plainly indicates that a land communication must have existed since the origin of the species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how identical or closely-related species across islands imply former terrestrial connections; cite shallow sea depths, ranges of volcanoes, and geological features (e.g. the 100-fathom line) as vera causa supporting biogeographical inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare species-composition across islands to infer sequence of separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Java possesses more birds and insects peculiar to itself than either Sumatra or Borneo, and this would indicate that it was earliest separated from the continent; next in organic individuality is Borneo, while Sumatra is so nearly identical ... that we may safely conclude it to have been the most recently dismembered island.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relative degrees of endemism and similarity to adjacent continents/islands to argue which landmasses separated earlier or later; give concrete examples of taxa and their distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame local narrative with generalizations/theory
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be thought that the facts and generalizations here given would have been more appropriately placed at the end rather than at the beginning of a narrative of the travels which supplied the facts. ... I have found it impossible to give such an account as I desire of the natural history of the numerous islands ... without constant reference to these generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an initial general sketch or theoretical framework so subsequent island-by-island descriptions are intelligible and instructive; refer back to these generalizations throughout the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use birds (and other mobile taxa) as clear indicators of distributional limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Birds offer us one of the best means of determining the law of distribution; ... the Passeres ... are generally as strictly limited by straits and arms of the sea as are quadrupeds themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why particular taxonomic groups are especially informative (e.g., dispersal tendencies, ecological constraints) and use them as primary evidence when mapping biogeographical boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize abrupt contrasts to delimit biogeographical regions
rubrics_metrics.description: The great contrast between the two divisions of the Archipelago is nowhere so abruptly exhibited as on passing from the island of Bali to that of Lombock ... The strait is here fifteen miles wide, so that we may pass in two hours from one great division of the earth to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight sharp faunal and floral changes over short distances to make region boundaries salient; use striking island-to-island contrasts as illustrative hooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate geological/physical evidence with biological observations
rubrics_metrics.description: This close resemblance, joined with the fact of the wide extent of sea which separates them being so uniformly and remarkably shallow, and lastly, the existence of the extensive range of volcanoes ... all lead irresistibly to the conclusion that at a very recent geological epoch, the continent of Asia extended far beyond its present limits ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlate biological patterns with bathymetry, volcanic chains, and other physical evidence; present multiple independent lines of evidence to support historical reconstructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe human cultures and link ethnography to natural-history conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrasts of Races.--Before I had arrived at the conviction that the eastern and western halves of the Archipelago belonged to distinct primary regions of the earth, I had been led to group the natives of the Archipelago under two radically distinct races. ... The reason why exactly the same line does not limit both is sufficiently intelligible. Man has means of traversing the sea which animals do not possess;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include social, linguistic, and cultural observations and discuss how human movement, technology, and history may modify or complicate biogeographical patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid, concrete descriptive detail to bring places and people to life
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chinese merchant is generally a fat round-faced man with an important and business-like look. He wears the same style of clothing ... his long tail tipped with red silk hangs down to his heels. ... In the Chinese bazaar are hundreds of small shops ... You may buy gimlets at a penny each, white cotton thread at four balls for a halfpenny ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sensory, specific details of costume, objects, sounds, and behaviors (prices, tools, cries) to create authenticity and reader immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge collection methods, serendipity, and limits of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner in which I obtained one fine insect was curious, and indicates how fragmentary and imperfect a traveller's collection must necessarily be. ... I never saw another specimen of it, and it was only after twelve years had elapsed that a second individual reached this country ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about sampling methods, the role of chance, and the incompleteness of field collections; use anecdotes to illustrate the provisional nature of some inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support claims with specimen counts, concrete data, and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: In about two months I obtained no less than 700 species of beetles, a large proportion of which were quite new, and among them were 130 distinct kinds of the elegant Longicorns ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give numbers, specimen counts, dates, and taxonomic specifics to bolster credibility and allow readers to appreciate the scale and reliability of observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogies and thought-experiments to make large-scale processes intelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Now let us endeavour to imagine ... that a slow upheaval of the bed of the Atlantic should take place ... we might have an irregular archipelago ... The animals and plants inhabiting these islands would, however, certainly reveal this portion of their former history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ hypothetical scenarios and comparative analogies (e.g., possible future geological changes) to help readers visualize and understand mechanisms behind observed patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate broad theory with island-by-island detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Having given this general sketch of the subject, I shall be able to show how the same principles can be applied to the individual islands of a group, as to the whole Archipelago; and thereby make my account ... more interesting and more instructive than if treated as mere isolated facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance panoramic generalizations with focused local descriptions: use the general framework to interpret and give meaning to specific island accounts.
